## The Spec — Your First Line of Defense Against Misconfiguration

The spec defines what development teams configure. Every constraint you add here is a runtime error you prevent.

### Mandatory Rules

**1. SENSITIVE DATA → USE `--secret` FLAG**

Passwords, API keys, tokens, certificates — mark with `--secret`. This sets `x-ui-secret-ref` so the UI renders a secret picker:
```bash
raptor module set-spec --add db_password \
  --type string --title "Database Password" \
  --description "Password for the database" \
  --min-length 8 --max-length 128 --secret --required
# --sample is auto-generated for --secret fields as <wire-a-secret>
```

**2. NO UNIVERSAL DEFAULT → OVERRIDE-ONLY**

If a value cannot have a single sensible default across all environments, it MUST be `--override-only`:
- VPC CIDR block (10.0.0.0/16 in dev, 10.1.0.0/16 in prod)
- Region (us-east-1 for dev, eu-west-1 for prod)
- Domain name (dev.example.com vs prod.example.com)

**2a. RESOURCE NAME → DUAL-MODE OVERRIDE-ONLY**

A resource's cloud name (`bucket_name`, `topic_name`, instance id) is `--override-only` and NOT `--required`, so an empty value is valid and the module derives the name in Terraform (verbatim when set, `{resource}-{suffix}` when empty). This is what lets one module import an existing estate at 0-change AND provision a 2nd greenfield env in the same account/project without collisions. See /design-facets-module §5 for the rule and suffix-by-scope choice; see step 4 below for the `coalesce` + truncate/hash pattern.
```bash
raptor module set-spec --add bucket_name \
  --type string --title "Bucket Name" \
  --description "Override the bucket name; leave empty to derive a collision-safe name" \
  --min-length 3 --max-length 63 --override-only --ui-order 1
```

**3. KNOWN VALUES → ENUM, ALWAYS**

If the valid values are a finite, known set, use `--type enum`. Never use string for something that has 3-20 valid options: instance types, storage classes, regions, tiers, protocols, log levels. See design skill spec principles for rationale.

**4. KNOWN FORMAT → PATTERN**

If a string has a structure, add `--pattern` to validate it at input time instead of failing 20 minutes into a Terraform apply. See design skill spec principles for rationale.

**5. REFERENCES ANOTHER RESOURCE → `--output-type`**

If the field value should be an existing resource in the blueprint, use `--output-type` so the UI shows a dropdown picker.

### Field Types

| Type | Usage | Required constraints |
|------|-------|---------------------|
| `string` | Text values | Always set `--min-length`, `--max-length` |
| `number` | Numeric values | Always set `--min`, `--max` |
| `boolean` | On/off toggles | Consider `--default` |
| `enum` | Fixed choices | Requires `--values "val1,val2,val3"` |
| `textarea` | Multi-line text | Descriptions, policy documents, lists |
| `editor` | Code with syntax highlighting | Requires `--language` |
| `yaml-editor` | YAML config | Requires `--acknowledge-no-merge` |

### Common Patterns

```
CIDR blocks:    --pattern "^([0-9]{1,3}\.){3}[0-9]{1,3}/[0-9]{1,2}$"
AWS ARN:        --pattern "^arn:aws:[a-z0-9-]+:[a-z0-9-]*:[0-9]*:.*$"
DNS-safe names: --pattern "^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9.-]{1,61}[a-z0-9]$"
AWS access key: --pattern "^AKIA[A-Z0-9]{16}$"
Semver:         --pattern "^[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+$"
Port (string):  --pattern "^[0-9]{1,5}$"
```

### Flags Reference

| Flag | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `--title TEXT` | Field title shown in UI (required for all fields). |
| `--description TEXT` | Field description (required for all fields). |
| `--required` | Must be provided. Requires `--sample`. |
| `--secret` | Value is a secret — UI shows secret picker. |
| `--override-only` | No stack default — per-environment only. |
| `--output-type @ns/t` | Links to a resource type (UI dropdown picker). |
| `--default VALUE` | Stack-level default, overridable per env. |
| `--pattern REGEX` | Validates format at input time. |
| `--ui-order N` | Position in the UI form (1-based). |
| `-f DIR` | Module directory (default: current directory). Used with `set-spec`, `add-input`, etc. |
| `--name-length-limit N` | Maximum resource name length (default 40). Used with `raptor module init`. |

### Example: VPC Module Spec

```bash
raptor module set-spec --add cidr_block \
  --type string --title "VPC CIDR Block" \
  --description "CIDR block for the VPC (e.g., 10.0.0.0/16)" \
  --min-length 9 --max-length 18 \
  --pattern "^([0-9]{1,3}\.){3}[0-9]{1,3}/[0-9]{1,2}$" \
  --required --sample "10.0.0.0/16" --ui-order 1

raptor module set-spec --add az_count \
  --type enum --title "Availability Zones" \
  --description "Number of AZs to spread across" \
  --values "2,3" --required --sample "3" --ui-order 2

raptor module set-spec --add enable_nat \
  --type boolean --title "NAT Gateway" \
  --description "Enable NAT gateway for private subnet internet access" \
  --default true --ui-order 3

raptor module set-spec --add subnet_bits \
  --type number --title "Subnet Bits" \
  --description "Additional bits for subnet CIDR (e.g., 4 for /20 subnets)" \
  --min 2 --max 8 --default 4 --ui-order 4
```

### Example: Service Module Spec

```bash
raptor module set-spec --add instance_type \
  --type enum --title "Instance Type" \
  --description "Compute instance type" \
  --values "t3.micro,t3.small,t3.medium,t3.large,t3.xlarge" \
  --override-only --ui-order 1

raptor module set-spec --add database \
  --type string --title "Database" \
  --description "Postgres database for this service" \
  --min-length 1 --max-length 255 \
  --output-type @facets/postgres \
  --required --sample "main-db" --ui-order 2

raptor module set-spec --add replicas \
  --type number --title "Replicas" \
  --description "Number of pod replicas" \
  --min 1 --max 50 --override-only --ui-order 3

raptor module set-spec --add port \
  --type enum --title "Service Port" \
  --description "Port the service listens on" \
  --values "80,443,8080,8443,3000,5000" \
  --default "8080" --ui-order 4
```

## Development Workflow

**0. Set up a project type (if needed) and discover what exists**

Your design decisions should already be made. This step confirms the environment matches your design.

```bash
# Import a managed project type (skip if one already exists)
# Full-featured (with pre-built modules):
raptor import project-type --managed facets/aws
raptor import project-type --managed facets/gcp
raptor import project-type --managed facets/azure

# Minimal (cloud account only — add modules incrementally):
raptor import project-type --managed facets/empty

# Or import from a local clone with modules
raptor import project-type -f ./project-type/aws/project-type.yml \
  --modules-dir ./modules --outputs-dir ./outputs

# Discover what's available
raptor module discover --project-type <your-project-type>
```

**1. Create output types for missing modules**
```bash
# No providers:
raptor module create-output-type @custom/vpc -f schema.yaml --exposes-provider none

# With providers (attribute mappings required):
raptor module create-output-type @custom/cloud_account -f schema.yaml \
  --exposes-provider aws:hashicorp/aws:5.0.0 \
  --provider-attribute aws:region=attributes.aws_region \
  --provider-attribute aws:assume_role.role_arn=attributes.aws_iam_role
```

**2. Scaffold the module**
```bash
raptor module init \
  --intent s3 --flavor aws --version 0.1 \
  --cloud aws --description "S3 bucket with encryption" \
  --input account:@facets/cloud_account \
  --requires-provider "provider=aws;input=account" \
  --output-type @facets/s3
```

> **Note:** "intent" in `module init` is the same as "TYPE" in upload/publish commands (e.g., `--intent s3` produces TYPE=s3 in `raptor publish iac-module s3/aws/0.1`).

**3. Define what teams configure (spec fields)**
```bash
raptor module set-spec --add bucket_name \
  --type string --title "Bucket Name" --description "S3 bucket name" \
  --min-length 3 --max-length 63 --required --sample "my-bucket"
```

**4. Write your Terraform in `main.tf`**

Your design decisions are already made — inputs, spec fields, output types, and provider chains were determined in the design skill. See design skill for platform thinking philosophy.

**The known-after-apply rule.** A value that Terraform only learns during apply
(an ARN, an id, any `resource.attribute`) cannot be used in THREE places:

```
  for_each = { ... }        keys must be known at plan time
  count    = ...            same
  output map KEYS           same — { for b in aws_s3_bucket.x : b.arn => ... }
                            hits the same wall as for_each
```

Key by spec map keys or static identifiers instead — things the blueprint chose,
not things the cloud assigned.

`try()` and `coalesce()` do **not** rescue an unknown value. They pick between
values; they do not make an unknown one known at plan time. Wrapping an ARN in
`try()` to satisfy `for_each` fails exactly the same way. (This matters here
because the resource-name pattern below legitimately uses `coalesce` — that use
is fine, because both of its arguments are known at plan time.)

Prefer `for_each` over `count` for iterating over collections. Breaking this rule
produces "known after apply" errors that force targeted applies and break the
deployment flow.

**Dual-mode resource names** (see /design-facets-module §5 for the rule). For each resource name field, derive the effective name in a `local` — verbatim when the override is set, resource-first `${var.instance_name}-${suffix}` when empty. `var.instance_name` is the blueprint resource name (e.g. `main-db`, `api`), so leading with it groups a resource's variants across envs and keeps the identity readable if the name is later truncated. Pick the suffix by uniqueness scope:

```hcl
locals {
  # ACCOUNT/PROJECT-scoped → suffix = env name (short; account-unique is enough)
  topic_name = coalesce(var.instance.spec.topic_name, "${var.instance_name}-${var.environment.name}")

  # REGION/ZONE-scoped → NO suffix (same name is fine in another region; dodges name caps)
  db_instance_name = coalesce(var.instance.spec.instance_name, var.instance_name)

  # GLOBAL namespace (buckets, storage accounts) → suffix = env unique_name (project+env token);
  # truncate + hash when it would exceed the provider's name cap (63 for GCS/S3).
  _bucket_raw = coalesce(var.instance.spec.bucket_name, "${var.instance_name}-${var.environment.unique_name}")
  bucket_name = length(local._bucket_raw) <= 63 ? local._bucket_raw : format(
    "%s-%s", substr(local._bucket_raw, 0, 54), substr(sha256(local._bucket_raw), 0, 8))
}
```

The home/imported env pins the live name via a per-env override (so the base blueprint stays name-free); greenfield envs leave it empty and get a collision-safe derived name. This is exactly what keeps a 2nd env in the same account/project from colliding with the home env's project-global names (topics, SQL instances, buckets). The scaffolded `variables.tf` already hints `${var.environment.unique_name}-${var.instance_name}` — this convention flips it resource-first.

Modules must destroy cleanly without manual intervention. Set appropriate deletion policies so `terraform destroy` succeeds without leaving orphaned resources or blocking on dependencies. Examples: `force_destroy = true` on S3 buckets, `skip_final_snapshot = true` on RDS, `deletion_policy = "ABANDON"` on CloudSQL database users, `prevent_destroy = false` on resources that might otherwise block. When `raptor destroy environment` runs, every resource must tear down fully — a stuck destroy blocks the entire environment lifecycle.

Conversely, add `prevent_destroy = true` lifecycle rules on critical stateful resources (databases, persistent volumes, storage buckets with data) to guard against accidental destruction in production. Facets uses `--allow-destroy` on releases to override this when intentional.

**5. Fill in outputs.tf managed section**

The scaffolded outputs.tf has `output_attributes` and `output_interfaces` locals
with TODO placeholders. Replace these with Terraform expressions from your resources:
```hcl
locals {
  output_attributes = {
    bucket_arn  = aws_s3_bucket.this.arn
    bucket_name = aws_s3_bucket.this.id
  }
}
```

**6. Configure exposed providers if the output type declares them**
```bash
# Example: kubernetes cluster module exposing kubernetes + helm providers
raptor module set-output-provider --output default --provider kubernetes \
  --source hashicorp/kubernetes --version "2.23.0" \
  --attribute host=attributes.cluster_endpoint \
  --attribute cluster_ca_certificate=attributes.ca_cert \
  --attribute token=attributes.token

raptor module set-output-provider --output default --provider helm \
  --source hashicorp/helm --version "2.11.0" \
  --attribute kubernetes.host=attributes.cluster_endpoint \
  --attribute kubernetes.cluster_ca_certificate=attributes.ca_cert \
  --attribute kubernetes.token=attributes.token
```

**7. Validate**
```bash
raptor module validate
```

**8. Design review before upload**

Before uploading, re-read the /design-facets-module skill's Design Review Checklist and audit your module:
- Are inputs truly structural dependencies, or should some be spec fields?
- Are spec fields generic enough for a team you haven't met?
- Is anything hardcoded (env vars, ARNs, policies, names) that should be configurable?
- Are collections using typed objects (`field.{.*}.subfield`) or yaml-editor — not JSON strings? (Use `{.*}` not `*` — bare `*` creates a literal property, not a dynamic map)
- Does `raptor module validate` pass?

**9. Upload and map to project type**
```bash
# Dry run first
raptor create iac-module -f ./my-module --dry-run

# Upload as PREVIEW (only usable in test projects)
raptor create iac-module -f ./my-module --auto-create    # Auto-create intent if it doesn't exist

# Map to your project type
raptor create resource-type-mapping my-project-type --resource-type intent/flavor

# Test in a test project, then publish for production use
raptor publish iac-module intent/flavor/version

# Or upload and publish in one step (skip PREVIEW)
raptor create iac-module -f ./my-module --auto-create --publish
```

**Modules repo linked?** (`raptor get modules-repo`) Then the two publish
commands above are the escape hatch, not the path: commit on your feature
branch, push, open a PR, and CI publishes on merge — see
`/modules-repo-workflow`. Under `ENFORCE` a publish from outside a clone of the
linked repo is rejected; under `WARN` it succeeds but prints a provenance
warning.

**Git provenance:** when the module directory lives in a git work tree, the upload
automatically records its source (origin remote URL with credentials stripped, HEAD
commit) on the module — keep modules in a git repo and commit before publishing so
every published version traces back to a commit. A warning is printed if the work
tree is dirty. Override with `--git-url`/`--git-ref` (useful in CI or for ZIP
uploads); opt out with `--no-git-metadata`. View with `raptor get iac-module <ref> --history`.

## Quick Reference

**Discover & Inspect**
```bash
raptor module development-guide           # This guide
raptor module discover --project-type TYPE   # Show modules, output types, provider chains
raptor module get-output-type @facets/type   # View an output type's schema
raptor module show                           # View a module's current state
raptor module set-spec --show                # View current spec schema
raptor module download TYPE/FLAVOR/VERSION --project-type TYPE  # Download a module's source
raptor module download-all --project-type TYPE                  # Download all modules in project type
raptor module design-guide                # Module design guide (bundling vs separating)
```

**Build**
```bash
raptor module create-output-type [--dry-run]  # Create/update an output type (alias: update-output-type)
raptor module delete-output-type --yes    # Delete an output type
raptor module init                        # Scaffold a new module
raptor module set-spec --add              # Add a spec field
raptor module add-input                   # Add an input dependency
# Note: `init` uses `--requires-provider "provider=aws;input=account"` format.
# Post-init, `add-input` uses `--provider aws` flag directly.
raptor module add-output                  # Add an output type mapping
raptor module set-output-provider         # Configure an exposed provider
```

**Modify**
```bash
raptor module set-spec --remove           # Remove a spec field
raptor module remove-input                # Remove an input
raptor module remove-output               # Remove an output mapping
```

**Validate & Ship**
```bash
raptor module validate                              # Check everything before upload
raptor get modules-repo                             # Linked modules repo? Then publish via PR (see /modules-repo-workflow)
raptor create iac-module -f DIR                     # Upload as PREVIEW
raptor create iac-module -f DIR --publish           # Upload and publish immediately (unlinked orgs)
raptor create iac-module -f DIR --auto-create       # Auto-create intent if new
raptor create iac-module -f DIR --dry-run           # Validate without uploading
raptor publish iac-module TYPE/FLAVOR/VER           # Publish a PREVIEW module (unlinked orgs)
```

**Project Type Mapping** (after upload, add module to project type)
```bash
raptor create resource-type-mapping PROJECT_TYPE --resource-type intent/flavor
```

## Sensitive Values in Raptor Commands — NEVER Put Secrets in the Chat

**CRITICAL RULE: NEVER ask the user to type a sensitive value (password, token, API
key, secret) in the chat.** Typing it in chat means the LLM sees it — it will be stored
in conversation history and logs. This is forbidden regardless of which tool you use to
ask (AskUserQuestion, chat message, follow-up question — all forbidden for secrets).

**Mandatory workflow — no exceptions:**

You run under the user's own shell — there is no vault or modal here. Keep the secret
out of the chat by having the user put it in an environment variable in their terminal,
then reference the *variable* (never the value) in raptor commands:

```bash
# 1. The user runs this in their own terminal. `read -rs` reads at a silent prompt,
#    so the value is never pasted into the chat and never reaches the LLM or transcript:
read -rs MY_DB_PASS; export MY_DB_PASS

# 2. Reference the env var in the raptor command. The user's shell expands "$MY_DB_PASS"
#    locally — the literal value never appears in what you (the LLM) emit or log.
#    Secrets never take a stack-level --value — set them per environment:
raptor create variable MY_DB_PASS -p myproject --secret --env-values prod="$MY_DB_PASS"
```

If a value should not even transit an env var, ask the user to run the single sensitive
raptor command themselves and paste back only the (non-sensitive) result.

**If the user offers to type the value in chat, redirect them:**
"Please don't paste it in chat — export it in your shell (`read -rs MY_DB_PASS; export
MY_DB_PASS`) and I'll reference `$MY_DB_PASS`, so the value never enters our conversation."

The `--secret` flag marks the variable as sensitive in the Facets Control Plane
(masked in UI, not returned in plain-text API responses).

## Before Publishing — Offer Operational Actions (MANDATORY GATE)

**Do NOT upload or publish a module until you have offered the user operational
actions.** This gate fires on EVERY module build, even when the user never mentions
"actions" or "tekton" — the trigger is reaching the publish step, not a keyword.

Modules that provision infrastructure (databases, caches, clusters, services) almost
always warrant day-2 operational actions — restart, scale, flush, snapshot, rotate
credentials, download kubeconfig, etc. These are `facets_tekton_action_kubernetes` /
`facets_tekton_action_aws` Terraform resources written into `actions.tf`, and surface
as clickable buttons on every resource instance in the Facets UI.

Immediately before running `raptor create iac-module ... --publish` or
`raptor publish iac-module ...`:

1. Invoke the **module-actions** skill — it is the authoritative reference for action
   schema, credential injection, and patterns by module type.
2. Propose a table of candidate actions for THIS module type and ask the user to
   choose (NEVER implement them silently):

   ```
   I recommend these operational actions for your <module_type> module:

   | Action | Description | Type | Rationale |
   |--------|-------------|------|-----------|
   | ...    | ...         | K8s/AWS | ... |

   Which of these should I implement? Any others you'd like to add?
   ```

3. Write the selected actions into `actions.tf`, re-run `raptor module validate`,
   THEN upload/publish.

If the user explicitly declines, proceed to publish without actions. Actions are only
supported for AWS and Kubernetes resources — skip this gate entirely for modules that
target only Azure or GCP.
